lead: Crown lengthening and gingivectomy are dental surgical procedures that reshape the gum line so that more of the tooth shows. For appearance, they are used to treat a gummy smile (excessive gingival display), where a band of gum shows above the upper teeth when smiling, and to even out an uneven gum line or teeth that look short because gum covers part of the crown. By moving the gum margin upward, the procedure lengthens the visible teeth and changes their proportions, which can make the smile look more balanced [1][2][21].

Crown lengthening exposes more tooth by removing gum tissue and sometimes supporting bone, and is done for functional or aesthetic reasons [1]. Gingivectomy is the removal of part of the gum tissue and is described as the oldest surgical approach in periodontal therapy [2]. A 2024 review divides crown lengthening into functional (exposing decay, fractures or restorative margins) and esthetic (typically in the front teeth, to lengthen short teeth or refine an uneven gum contour) [14].

Both are established dental procedures used for restorative and periodontal reasons; their use for smile aesthetics is the part relevant to looksmaxxing. Most of the clinical literature on crown lengthening addresses restorative cases, and a 2018 review notes that the esthetic version in the front of the mouth is still a matter of debate with no single evidence-based technique [15]. Registered trials in 2011-2026 compare techniques such as flapless, piezoelectric, laser and digitally guided approaches [3][4][5].

chain: Gum tissue (and sometimes bone) is trimmed or repositioned higher on the teeth
More of each tooth crown is visible and less gum shows
Teeth look longer and the smile line looks more proportionate
angle.text: People with a gummy smile or short-looking teeth caused by gum overgrowth or delayed tooth eruption use the procedure to expose more of the tooth and reduce visible gum. The result is a permanent change to the gum line.

paras: Crown lengthening may be done surgically by an apically repositioned flap with bone recontouring, or orthodontically by forced tooth eruption [1]. In the flap approach, the gum is lifted, bone is reshaped at a more apical level and the gum is repositioned; it suits several teeth at once and gives immediate exposure of tooth structure but can be painful. Forced eruption uses braces to pull the tooth coronally before surgery, preserving bone on adjacent teeth but requiring a fixed appliance and a longer treatment [1]. Gingivectomy can be performed with a scalpel, electrosurgery or laser [2].

Surgeons work around the supracrestal tissue attachment, historically called biologic width, the band of gum attachment above the bone crest. Wikipedia reports an average of about 2 mm, with a range of roughly 0.75 to 4.3 mm, and that surgeons often leave at least 3 mm of tooth and gum above the bone crest [1]. A human study of 23 patients found that bone removal of 1 to 5 mm was followed by the biologic width being re-established at its original vertical dimension by 6 months, with a consistent 3 mm gain of coronal tooth structure [19].

Wikipedia states that up to about 3 mm of gum display when smiling is considered acceptable and more is often regarded as unaesthetic, and that gingivectomy can address it [2]. Another Wikipedia article on gummy smile defines it as more than 2 mm of gum above the upper central incisors in a full smile, reports it in about 10 percent of US adults aged 20 to 30 and notes it is more common in women [21]. Aesthetic planning must consider smile line, lip position and tooth proportions [2], and symmetry of left and right tooth lengths may require treating more teeth than first planned [1].

A gummy smile has several possible causes: delayed passive eruption of the teeth, overactive upper-lip elevator muscles, excessive vertical growth of the upper jaw, over-eruption of the upper front teeth, or a combination [21]. Crown lengthening or gingivectomy addresses cases where excess gum or delayed passive eruption is the cause; other causes are addressed with other options listed in the same article, such as orthodontics, botulinum toxin in the lip muscles (effects averaging about six months) or fat transplantation [21]. Trials in the area treat altered passive eruption, the condition in which the gum margin stays too far down the crown [6][7].

Soreness usually resolves within one to two weeks [1]. The gum margin can migrate back toward the crown after surgery. A 2010 review reports that an average of 3 mm of supragingival soft tissue rebounds coronal to the bone crest, taking at least three months to complete, and advises waiting at least three months, and possibly six in aesthetically important areas, before final restorations [20]. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of four controlled trials (182 procedures in 111 participants) found stable periodontal tissue levels over 3 to 6 months, although clinical attachment level changes at 6 months favoured adjacent untreated teeth, and called for more evidence [16].

Described drawbacks include encroaching on the supracrestal tissue attachment, weakening adjacent teeth by removing bone, bone loss that is hard to restore, and postoperative pain with the flap technique [1]. Lost bone is almost impossible to restore fully, which may limit later options such as implants [1]. For gingivectomy, recurrence, black triangles and return of disease with poor hygiene are described [2]. A 2010 review notes that osseous resection could affect periodontal stability and may be a contraindication in some cases [20].

A 2024 randomized trial of 16 patients with altered passive eruption type 1B compared conventional esthetic crown lengthening with a 3D-printed dual surgical guide. Wound healing, pain and gingival margin stability did not differ over 6 months, while operating time was significantly shorter with the guide [17]. A trial of 62 patients (230 anterior teeth) compared three methods of making crown-extension guides and reported fewer follow-up visits, less guide-design time and shorter surgery in the digital groups [18].

Registered trials include a comparison of periodontal plastic surgery techniques for gummy smile (n=30) [8], digitally guided versus conventional crown lengthening [9][10], flapless esthetic crown lengthening for excessive gingival display (n=28, 2011) [11], closed piezoelectric versus open flap approaches [12][13], Er:YAG laser versus surgical crown lengthening [4] and periodontal stability after correcting altered passive eruption [7]. Results of these registrations have not been summarized here.

timeline.event: Human study documents re-establishment of biologic width and a 3 mm gain of tooth structure 3 to 6 months after surgery [19].
Registered trial of flapless esthetic crown lengthening for excessive gingival display begins [11].
Periodontology 2000 review notes esthetic crown lengthening technique remains debated [15].
Randomized trial of 3D-printed guides for esthetic crown lengthening is published [17].

refs.title: Gummy smile

name: Crown lengthening / gingivectomy

card.summary: Dental surgery that trims gum (and sometimes bone) to expose more tooth, used for gummy smiles when the gum line is the cause.
card.note: Bone removal is irreversible and can affect adjacent teeth.

quick.overview:
Crown lengthening and gingivectomy remove gum tissue, and in some cases bone, to expose more of the teeth. They are standard periodontal procedures also used to reduce gum display in a smile.

Registered trials compare surgical, flapless, piezoelectric, laser and digitally guided methods.
quick.mechanism: Gum is trimmed or repositioned, with bone recontouring if needed, so the gum line sits higher on the teeth.
quick.risks: Described drawbacks include irreversible bone loss, weakening of neighbouring teeth, pain with flap surgery, recurrence and black triangles.
